properties.decision:
RECORDED AS BRAINSTORMING, NOT AS A PROPOSAL (Anthony, 2026-10-27): "Does symbolic math now allow us to do physics or the application of math to a phenomenon? The sinogram test case is really physics test case where we are trying to reconstruct something we observe. I work at NSLS-II and it is a bunch of scientists applying math. At Brookhaven National Labs, I have friends that work in quantum physics - I think being able to layout the phenomenon they observe or hypothesize and use actual symbolic math to represent the problem is very powerful. Now we have lines of reason that support scientific theory. Like we are designing experiments. This would be very helpful in writing a scientific journal article for instance. Again, this is the partnership between flo2-calc and reflow2 that is capturing the design and math to support their hypothesis."

What already stands (accepted): calc's req:the-math-of-a-study-is-designed-up-front (a study's math is designed before the data, the verdict follows rules fixed in advance), power and sample size up front, a test's criteria changed after its data are reported; the served skill "design the math of a study" is PLANNED, not built; lines of reasoning (design-an-argument) and proofs (design-a-proof) are served. What this adds is the PHENOMENON layer between them: the observation or hypothesis, the model (its equations, each assumption and the regime where it holds), the derivation from model to a predicted observable (symbolic steps checked, conditions stated), the predicted numbers with uncertainty (calc), the experiment that would discriminate between rival models, and the comparison with data, all as one line of reasoning a paper's sections can be read out of.

Options as they came up (none chosen):
(a) A served skill "design a phenomenon / an experiment" composing what exists: argument lines for the hypothesis and rivals, calc records for each prediction, the study-up-front skill for the test, and symbolic checks (once built) for derivation steps.
(b) The model's equations as first-class records (symbols with units and meaning, assumptions, regime of validity), so a changed assumption re-derives every prediction resting on it (live formulas, accepted 10-27) and propagate_change names the claims it weakens.
(c) A read-out of the design as a paper skeleton: introduction from the observation and rivals, methods from the experiment design, results from the data records, discussion from what the line of reasoning reads supported, refuted or conditional.
(d) Trial it first on a real case: the sinogram reconstruction design (reconstructing an object from what a beamline observes), then a willing physicist's own hypothesis.

Counter-arguments kept beside it:
- Most real physics models are not closed-form: quantum many-body problems, PDEs, Monte Carlo, fits to data need numerical codes (and Mathematica, Julia, Python stacks scientists already trust). Symbolic math checks derivations and small models; the value here is the traceable reasoning and checked steps around their codes, with those codes' outputs as cited records, not replacing them.
- A CAS checks algebra, never physical validity: an approximation's regime, a neglected term, a boundary condition. Those must stay stated assumptions, read as conditions, or a design will look more proven than it is (shown on the heat-equation step in the 10-27 proof of concept).
- Confidentiality: unpublished hypotheses and data are exactly what scientists guard. Until flo2.io's confidentiality ideas (operator cannot read designs; metrics not content) are settled, this suits public or published work, or a self-hosted reflow2.
- Scope: this is reflow2's "design anything" applied to science; the cheapest real step is (d)+(a), composing what exists, before any new record type (b) or read-out (c).
properties.name: SETTLED 2026-10-27 — a phenomenon is designed by trialling it first on the sinogram reconstruction design (d), then writing a served skill that composes what exists (a); equations as first-class records (b) and a paper read-out (c) stay considered
